transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is that over the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always doing something—puttering around, fixing little things, arranging things, signing up to help with one more thing. Even at my age, I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you feel restless when you're not doing something?

Yes, I do. Like at the senior center meetings, or when I’m sitting through the announcements at church, I get this ants-in-my-chair feeling. I end up shifting around, getting up for coffee, or straightening papers just so I can sit through it.
Do you feel anxious when you're not keeping busy?
I’m not sure I’d call it anxious, exactly. I just notice I don’t like sitting idle for long. I feel better when I’ve got something to do with my hands or some little task to take care of.
Do you have thoughts that repeat over and over in your mind?
No, I don’t think so. I don’t really get stuck on one thought going around and around. It’s more that I just notice when I’m sitting there with nothing to do, but not repeated thoughts, no.
Do you think you keep busy to avoid feeling upset or uncomfortable?
I don’t think so. It doesn’t feel like I’m trying to avoid being upset. I just don’t like sitting around with nothing to do, that’s all.
Has this need to keep busy been a part of your life for as long as you can remember?

Yes, I think it has. I can remember back in grade school getting scolded for popping out of my seat or talking over other children. They’d say I was “too lively,” things like that. So yes, it goes back a long way, before I was a teenager.
Do you ever feel like you have to perform certain rituals or routines in a specific way?
No, I don’t think so. I have ordinary routines, like anyone, but I don’t feel like I have to do them in some exact way or something bad will happen.
Do you find that you get even busier when you're under stress or upset?

I don’t know that stress makes it much worse. It’s more that, in this past year or so, I’m just always puttering around—fixing little things, arranging things, volunteering for one more thing. Even at my age, I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you think your need to stay busy helps you deal with stress?

Maybe a little, but I don’t really think of it that way. It’s more like I just keep moving—puttering around, fixing little things, arranging things, saying yes to one more thing. If I sit down too long, I feel restless, like I should be doing something.
Has your need to keep busy ever caused problems for you at work, at home, or in your relationships with others?

Yes, a little. At the senior center, I’ve had to apologize after meetings because I got too wound up or made things tense. One friend even suggested I take a smaller role at the sign-up table, because the way I was handling things was upsetting people a bit.
Do you feel like your constant need to stay busy is interfering with your relationships or daily life in a significant way?

Yes, somewhat. I wouldn’t say it’s ruining my life, but it has caused some trouble. At the senior center I’ve had to apologize after meetings, and a friend suggested I take a smaller role at the sign-up table because I was making things tense. So yes, it does get in the way a bit.
Do you feel like your constant need to stay busy is causing you a lot of distress?

It does bother me, yes. I don’t know if I’d call it a lot of distress every day, but it’s enough that I came in about it. For the past year or so I feel like I’m always puttering, fixing something, arranging things, or signing up to help with one more thing. Even at 87, I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you feel like you could stop being busy if you really wanted to?

I think I could slow down for a little while if I really made myself, but it doesn’t feel natural. I just keep finding things to putter with or fix or arrange, or I’ll sign up to help with something else. Even now, at 87, sitting still is hard for me.
Do you feel like something bad would happen if you didn't complete the tasks or activities you start?
No, I don’t think so. It’s not like I’m afraid something terrible will happen if I don’t finish. I just feel pulled to keep doing things, and it’s hard to leave something alone once I’ve started.
Has your level of busyness increased or decreased as you've gotten older?

I’d say it’s been more noticeable this past year. I’ve always liked to keep busy, but lately I’m puttering, fixing things, arranging things, or volunteering for one more thing more than I used to. And at 87, I still have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Has your need to keep busy changed significantly over the course of your life?

It’s been there in some form, I think, but it’s gotten more noticeable this past year or so. I’m always puttering around, fixing things, arranging something, or saying yes to one more volunteer thing. Even at my age, I just don’t sit still very easily.
Do you think your busy behavior is something you've learned to do over time or is it just part of who you are?

I think it’s more just part of who I am, though it’s become more noticeable lately. This past year or so, I’m always puttering around, fixing or arranging something, or signing up to help with one more thing. Even at 87, I still have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you feel like you're in control of when you start and stop your busy activities?

Not always, no. I can decide to start something, but once I get going—puttering, fixing things, arranging something—it’s hard for me to just stop and sit down. I’ll tell myself I’m only doing one more thing, and then I’ve volunteered for something else or found another little job to do. At 87, I still don’t settle very easily.
